title: Choose a Model for the Task
subtitle: Compare approved options in GitHub Copilot for VS Code

scenes.title: Define a small benchmark
scenes.body: Compare options on work that you can independently verify.
scenes.narration: Let’s compare two models on the same bug. The baseline function accepts zero. The issue says one and five should pass, while zero and negative one should fail. We ask for a cause, a small fix, and one regression test. Before opening either chat, write these expectations down. That gives both answers the same standard.
scenes.code:
Issue: reject zero quantities.
Keep the function signature.
Expected: 1 and 5 pass, 0 and -1 fail.
scenes.result: Score the response against those requirements.
scenes.focus: The four expected outcomes define the comparison
scenes.action: Copy the issue and list its expected outcomes.

scenes.title: Check the Copilot model picker
scenes.body: Choose from the options your work account exposes.
scenes.narration: Open the model picker in Copilot Chat. Choose two options actually available in your managed workspace and record their labels. Use the same session mode for both. If your account offers one model, run it twice to see whether the answer stays consistent. Record those as two attempts with the same model.
scenes.code:
Open Copilot Chat.
Inspect the model selection options.
Record model A and model B as displayed.
scenes.result: Availability depends on your work configuration.
scenes.focus: Two actual picker labels identify the candidates
scenes.action: Record the labels of two approved models in Copilot Chat.

scenes.title: Use the same task and context
scenes.body: Start separate chats and attach the same files.
scenes.narration: Use two fresh Plan sessions on the same revision. In each, attach the issue, the validator, and its tests. Paste the same prompt. Ask why zero passes, then request a minimal fix and one regression test. Leave edits out of this comparison. If a run sees more source or uses a different mode, record that difference before interpreting its result.
scenes.code:
Explain why zero is accepted.
Propose a minimal fix and one regression test.
Keep the signature. Describe changes only.
scenes.result: Repeat with the same issue and attached files.
scenes.focus: The prompt and attachments match in both runs
scenes.action: Run the same Plan prompt in two fresh chats.

scenes.title: Score observable differences
scenes.body: Compare evidence, scope, verification, and response time.
scenes.narration: Example A identifies equality, proposes a zero test, and keeps the existing interface. Example B also finds the cause, but adds a refactor the issue never asked for. Both may sound polished. Score the substance first. Only then look at the example response times. Those numbers describe these illustrative runs and can vary across attempts and sessions.
scenes.code:
A: correct cause, focused test, 6 s.
B: correct cause, extra refactor, 15 s.
Synthetic sample results
scenes.result: Both found the defect. A stayed in scope.
scenes.focus: Correct cause and tighter scope distinguish the sample outputs
scenes.action: Score each sample against the same criteria.

scenes.title: Start with a suitable option
scenes.body: Use stronger reasoning when a clear capability gap appears.
scenes.narration: For this task, the smaller proposal is easier to review because the expected behavior is explicit. A larger migration may justify evaluating a stronger reasoning option on a representative task. You can make that choice from several runs and the evidence they produce. In this small exercise, the best signal is whether the suggested regression catches the defect.
scenes.code:
Small, clear change → try a fast option.
Complex or uncertain change → evaluate reasoning.
For either option → verify with evidence.
scenes.result: Use task demands and results to guide the choice.
scenes.focus: A narrow task favors a suitable, verifiable choice
scenes.action: Select a model for the small fix and name why.

scenes.title: Confirm the test can catch the bug
scenes.body: The quality score depends on checking the proposed result.
scenes.narration: Compare two test ideas. A test that expects one to pass stays green on the buggy revision. A test that expects zero to fail exposes the equality bug. Run the chosen assertion on the original code in an approved runner. Then apply the small fix and repeat the test. Seeing red first and green afterward makes the model comparison concrete.
scenes.code:
Test idea 1: verify that quantity 1 passes.
Test idea 2: verify that quantity 0 fails.
Run each against the original validator.
scenes.result: The zero test detects this specific defect.
scenes.focus: The zero test fails on the buggy revision
scenes.action: Run the proposed zero assertion against the baseline.

scenes.title: Write a short conclusion
scenes.body: Name the model and explain your evidence.
scenes.narration: Write a short decision a teammate can repeat. Name the two model labels, the task, the shared inputs, and the evidence you used. You might say Example A was easier to review because it preserved the signature and produced a test that failed on the original. Repeat the comparison on another small task before treating one result as a general preference.
scenes.code:
Task: zero quantity boundary
Compared: actual model labels
Decision: what performed well and why
Evidence: expected regression result
scenes.result: A reproducible choice you can revisit.
scenes.focus: A short decision cites behavior and evidence
scenes.action: Record your model choice with a reproducible reason.
